packages/contracts/package.json.content: The declared entrypoints resolve into `./dist`, but the repo `.gitignore` ignores `dist/` and there is no `.npmignore` or `files` allowlist. npm falls back to `.gitignore` when packing, so a published/installed tarball would exclude `dist/` entirely, leaving `main`/`types` pointing at non-existent files (`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for consumers). There is also no `prepare`/`prepublishOnly` script, so `dist` may not even be built at publish time. Add a `files` allowlist including `dist` and a build hook, e.g. `"files": ["dist"]` plus `"prepublishOnly": "yarn build"` (or `"prepare": "tsc -p tsconfig.json"`).

Unlike sibling packages that define an explicit `exports` map (e.g. `packages/controller-flx4/package.json`), this `"type": "module"` package exposes only `main`/`types`. Any future subpath entry (or tooling that requires an `exports` field) will fail to resolve, and there is no conditional `require`/`import` boundary. Consider adding an `exports` map for consistency and forward-compatibility.

packages/controller-flx4/package.json.content: `build` runs `tsc -p tsconfig.json`, whose `include` is the whole `src` directory (which contains `*.test.ts`) and which has no test exclude; combined with the absence of a `files` allowlist or `private` flag here, the build emits `dist/*.test.js` / `dist/*.test.d.ts` and a publish would ship test artifacts, source maps and `vitest.config.ts`. Add an `exclude` for test files in tsconfig, or constrain the publish surface with a `files` array (e.g. `["dist"]`) / `"private": true` if the package is internal-only.

packages/govee/src/scenes.ts.content: Prototype-chain lookup bug. `catalog.scenes[name]` is a plain-object property read that also walks the prototype chain. For names like `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `toString` the lookup returns an inherited member (truthy, and `constructor` even has `length === 1`), so both guards pass and `[...scene]` then throws `TypeError: scene is not iterable`. The function is documented to return `null` for unknown scenes, so a user/service-supplied scene name can crash the resolver instead of producing the expected error result. Guard with an own-property check and an `Array.isArray` check (which also defends against a malformed catalogue where the value is a non-iterable/truthy object).

Producer/parser asymmetry (round-trip is not idempotent). `ptRealCommand` happily serializes an empty `command` array and empty-string entries, but `parsePtRealCommand` rejects both (`command.length === 0` and `entry.length > 0`). So a datagram produced by `ptRealCommand` can fail to parse back via `parsePtRealCommand`. Since `sceneFromCatalog` only rejects empty arrays, a catalogue entry such as `[""]` still yields a wire datagram that the parser (e.g. when reading an echo/ack of the same shape) returns `null` for, which is easy to mistake for a malformed reply. Align the validation on both sides (reject empty/invalid entries at produce time, or tolerate them at parse time).

packages/matter/src/controller.test.ts.content: This is the only failure assertion for the post-close path, and it omits `name`. `toMatchObject({ reason: "stopped" })` performs a partial match, so any rejected value carrying a `reason: "stopped"` property (a plain object, a differently-named Error subclass, or the wrong error type) satisfies it. Since the sibling negative test asserts `name: "MatterError"`, this one should do the same so it actually verifies the typed error contract.

`adapter.close()` is the last statement of every test, so a failing assertion above it skips cleanup entirely. If this ever runs against a real adapter (the file explicitly says the in-memory adapter stands in for a matter.js-backed one) this leaks sockets/subscriptions and can contaminate later tests, and it also means the close/teardown path is never exercised when a test fails. Prefer creating the adapter in a helper and closing it in an `afterEach` or a `try/finally`.

This try/catch block is redundant and can mask the real failure. The same `command(99, ...)` call is already asserted twice above with `.rejects.toMatchObject(...)`. If the call ever resolves, `expect.unreachable()` throws its own error which is swallowed by `catch` and then re-checked with `toBeInstanceOf(MatterError)` — the test fails, but the reported cause points to the wrong assertion rather than to the command resolving unexpectedly. Remove the block (or replace with a single explicit `rejects.toBeInstanceOf(MatterError)` assertion) instead of re-invoking the command a third time.

Rejection coverage for `classifyPairingCode` is thin and misses the boundary cases most likely to regress: 11-character strings containing non-digits (e.g. `"1234567890a"`), longer/shorter digit runs (`"123456789012"`, `"1234567890"`), a `MT:` prefix followed by characters outside `[A-Z0-9.+-]`, and lower/mixed-case `mt:` payloads. Because the validator strips spaces/dashes before the digit check, inputs such as a trailing separator (`"12345678901-"`) also misclassify as `manual-code`; without a test pinning the intended behaviour, such defects pass CI unnoticed.

The test bakes in the internal `nextNodeId` sequence (always 1 for a fresh adapter) and never verifies the id contract itself. A regression where ids collide across commissions or leak across adapter instances would go undetected. Consider commissioning twice and asserting the second id is distinct/incremented, and asserting that two separate adapters do not share id space.
